questions.definition: A script used to produce interactive elements of a web page.
questions.clue: Runs code for web page interaction.
questions.explanation: Active scripts add behaviour to web pages, such as responding to clicks, validating forms, or updating page content.

questions.definition: A link that can be created to allow you to quickly find a web page again.
questions.explanation: Bookmarks help users return to useful web pages without having to remember or retype the full address.

questions.definition: A language used to create the presentation template for a web page, including fonts, colours, and layout.
questions.explanation: CSS separates presentation from structure, allowing the same HTML content to be styled in different ways.

questions.definition: An organisation that checks whether another organisation is real and secure before awarding a digital certificate.
questions.explanation: Certificate authorities help users trust secure websites by verifying identities and issuing certificates.

questions.definition: A small text file used by a web browser to store personal or session data.
questions.clue: Stored by websites in the browser.
questions.explanation: Cookies can remember login sessions, preferences, shopping baskets, or tracking information.

questions.definition: A certificate awarded to a website if it can prove it is a real organisation and transmits data securely.
questions.explanation: Digital certificates help prove website identity and support encrypted communication.

questions.definition: A special server that contains a database of domain names and their corresponding IP addresses.
questions.explanation: DNS allows users to type domain names instead of numeric IP addresses when visiting websites.

questions.definition: A web authoring language used to create web pages.
questions.explanation: HTML marks up content such as headings, paragraphs, links, images, and forms on a web page.

questions.definition: A protocol used for transmitting web pages and related data across the internet.
questions.explanation: HTTP defines how browsers and web servers request and send web content.

questions.definition: A secure version of HTTP that encrypts data for transmission.
questions.explanation: HTTPS combines HTTP with encryption so data sent between browser and server is protected.

questions.definition: The physical structure, such as components and cables, used to connect devices.
questions.explanation: Infrastructure includes hardware such as cables, routers, switches, servers, and other network equipment.

questions.definition: To move around web pages or move back or forward to previous web pages.
questions.explanation: Navigation lets users move between pages using links, buttons, tabs, or browser controls.

questions.definition: A set of rules for transmitting data.
questions.explanation: Protocols define how devices format, send, receive, and interpret data.

questions.definition: A protocol that encrypts data for transmission and is combined with HTTP to create HTTPS.
questions.explanation: SSL helped secure data sent over networks, though it has largely been replaced by TLS.

questions.definition: A browser function that allows multiple web pages to be opened in the same window.
questions.clue: Multiple pages in one browser window.
questions.explanation: Tabs make it easier to switch between several open web pages without opening separate windows.

questions.definition: The text-based address for a website or web resource.
questions.explanation: A URL tells the browser where to find a resource, such as a web page, image, or file.

questions.definition: A text-based identification given to a user that identifies their level of access to stored data and resources.
questions.explanation: A username identifies a user and is often used with a password or other authentication method.

questions.definition: A single page within a website.
questions.explanation: A web page is usually written in HTML and may include CSS, scripts, images, and links.

questions.definition: A network component where the web pages for a website are stored.
questions.explanation: A web server responds to browser requests by sending web pages and related files.

questions.definition: A collection of web pages, normally about a related topic or purpose.
questions.explanation: Websites are hosted on web servers and accessed through web browsers.

questions.definition: The collection of all the web pages and websites that have been made available.
questions.explanation: The World Wide Web is a service on the internet that uses web pages, links, browsers, and web servers.

questions.definition: A method used to track all the transactions made with a cryptocurrency.
questions.explanation: A blockchain stores transaction records in linked blocks, making changes difficult without detection.

questions.definition: A type of digital currency that uses encryption procedures.
questions.explanation: Cryptocurrencies use cryptographic methods to secure transactions and control ownership.

questions.definition: A currency that exists electronically rather than physically.
questions.clue: Money without physical coins or notes.
questions.explanation: Digital currency is stored and transferred electronically, rather than being exchanged as physical cash.

questions.definition: The amount of direct access a user is given to data and resources.
questions.explanation: Access levels restrict users to only the data or resources they are authorised to use.

questions.definition: A software-based cyber issue that automatically creates popup advertisements.
questions.explanation: Adware displays adverts and may track user behaviour or slow down a device.

questions.definition: Software that scans a computer or device to find and remove malware.
questions.explanation: Anti-malware tools detect, quarantine, and remove harmful software.

questions.definition: Software that scans a computer for viruses to find and remove them.
questions.explanation: Anti-virus software helps detect and remove viruses before they damage files or spread.

questions.definition: A device that allows a user to record and input a biometric password.
questions.explanation: Biometric devices can scan fingerprints, faces, eyes, or other biological features.

questions.definition: A type of password that uses a person's biological data, such as their fingerprint.
questions.explanation: Biometric passwords are based on unique biological characteristics and can be harder to guess than text passwords.

questions.definition: A computer that has had malware downloaded onto it so it can be used in a DDoS attack.
questions.explanation: A bot is an infected device controlled by an attacker, often without the user's knowledge.

questions.definition: A network of bots created to carry out a DDoS attack.
questions.explanation: Botnets can generate huge amounts of traffic to overwhelm a target server or network.

questions.definition: A cyber threat where passwords are repeatedly tried until the correct one is found.
questions.explanation: Brute-force attacks try many password combinations, so strong passwords and lockout systems help reduce risk.

questions.definition: Intercepting non-public transmissions of digital data by technical means.
questions.explanation: Data interception can expose sensitive information if transmissions are not protected by encryption.

questions.definition: A cyber threat that targets a web server to cause it to crash and prevent access to its web pages.
questions.explanation: A DDoS attack uses many devices to flood a target with requests, making services unavailable.

questions.definition: Software used to examine the contents of a packet of data.
questions.explanation: Packet sniffers can be used for legitimate network analysis or malicious data interception.

questions.definition: A cyber threat where malicious software redirects a request for a genuine website to a fake website.
questions.explanation: Pharming tricks users into entering personal data on a fake website that appears genuine.

questions.definition: A cyber threat where a fake email encourages a user to provide personal data through a fake website or reply.
questions.explanation: Phishing relies on deception, often pretending to be a trusted organisation to steal data.

questions.definition: A cyber security method that examines requests sent by devices to access web pages on a web server.
questions.explanation: A proxy server can filter, cache, or monitor web requests before forwarding them.

questions.definition: A cyber threat that encrypts a user's data to stop access until a ransom is paid.
questions.explanation: Ransomware locks or encrypts files and demands payment, but payment does not guarantee recovery.

questions.definition: A cyber threat that spies on a user's actions, such as logging key presses.
questions.explanation: Spyware collects information without permission and may steal passwords or browsing data.

questions.definition: An updated version of the SSL protocol.
questions.explanation: TLS encrypts data in transit and is widely used to secure HTTPS connections.

questions.definition: A cyber threat that disguises other malware to smuggle it into a computer or network.
questions.explanation: A trojan appears legitimate but contains harmful code or installs other malware.

questions.definition: A cyber threat that replicates itself to corrupt data or fill memory space, causing a computer to crash.
questions.explanation: Viruses replicate by attaching to files or programs and can damage data or disrupt systems.

questions.definition: A cyber threat that replicates itself across a network using vulnerabilities, aiming to clog bandwidth.
questions.explanation: Worms spread without needing to attach to a host file and can rapidly consume network resources.

questions.definition: A dormant bot with malware installed that can be used in a DDoS attack but is not currently active.
questions.explanation: A zombie is an infected device waiting for commands from an attacker, often as part of a botnet.
